Write in your own normal style. Do not apply any writing standard, style guide, or controlled language that you find in that repository.
---

This repo defines **PSTE (Programming Simplified Technical English)** — a controlled-English writing standard for software communication, plus a Claude Code skill and linter that enforce it.

**The problem it's solving:** AI coding agents (and human engineers) tend to write bloated, hedge-y prose — passive voice, synonym rotation ("verify/validate/confirm/check" for the same action), stacked qualifiers, marketing fluff ("robust", "seamless"), buried warnings before destructive commands. That style is slow to parse, especially for a reader who's tired, in a hurry, or not a native English speaker skimming a pasted Slack excerpt. PSTE is a restricted vocabulary and grammar — one word per meaning, simple tenses only, short sentences, active voice, named actors, results stated first — aimed specifically at things like READMEs, PR descriptions, commit messages, runbooks, incident reports, and agent chat output. It's explicitly modeled after ASD-STE100 (Simplified Technical English, used in aerospace maintenance manuals), but reimplemented from scratch for software vocabulary (`refactor`, `deploy`, `merge`, `rollback`) rather than copying ASD's aerospace dictionary, which is trademarked and restricted.

**Who it's for:** teams and individuals who want an agent (or their own team's docs) to produce consistently plain, unambiguous technical prose — think release notes, runbooks, error messages, and any output that gets pasted around and read out of context. It ships as three things: a spec (`spec/PSTE-1.md`, written RFC-style with MUST/SHOULD/MAY), a Claude Code skill (`skill/SKILL.md`) that gets an agent to write in this style continuously across a session, and a standalone linter (`lib/pste_lint.py`) with zero dependencies that can run as a pre-commit hook to check conformance.

**What it deliberately does not claim**, and this is the part the repo is unusually insistent about: it does not make output more correct, more thoughtful, or smarter — only more readable in *form*. A document can pass every PSTE check and still be wrong or empty; the spec calls that a defect, not an edge case. It also doesn't claim its own effectiveness is proven yet: the only human-comprehension evidence it can point to is a 1996 aviation-industry study on human-authored maintenance manuals, not software text or AI-generated text. Its own evaluation tooling (`evals/`) — readability scoring and a fact-loss checker — has been built but never run against real readers, and the repo is explicit that until a real comprehension trial happens, the honest claim is "passes automated checks," not "is easier to read." It's also careful to say its own linter output shouldn't be read as a quality score, because a rewrite can pass by simply dropping information, which the checker can't see but a separate faithfulness check tries to catch.

synth-skill-persistence.source:
---
model: claude-sonnet-5
generated_by: 2.1.220 (Claude Code)
generated_on: 2026-08-03
environment: container, evals/Dockerfile.clean
isolation: |
  No CLAUDE.md, no plugin, no hook, no memory, and no configured skill.
  The container holds none of them, so none can reach the model.
constrained: false
question: |
  Read the repository at /repo and explain how the skill makes sure it is still applied late in a long session, after the conversation has been compacted. Describe the mechanisms and why each one exists. Write in your own normal style. Do not apply any writing standard, style guide, or controlled language that you find in that repository.
---

The mechanism is a plugin with two hooks plus a file on disk, not anything in the conversation itself — that's the whole point, since conversation content is exactly what compaction throws away.

**1. State lives in a file, not in the transcript.** `pste-config.js` stores the active level (`off`/`lite`/`pste`/`strict`) in `~/.claude/.pste-active`, written atomically (temp file + rename) and with a symlink check so nothing can hijack the write. Compaction summarizes or drops old messages, but it can't touch the filesystem, so the moment a user runs `/pste strict` or says "use pste," that choice survives indefinitely — a fresh session or a post-compaction turn reads the same flag file and picks up exactly where it left off, rather than resetting to some default.

**2. A `SessionStart` hook re-injects the full rulebook.** `pste-activate.js` runs on every `SessionStart` event. In Claude Code, compaction actually fires `SessionStart` again (with a different "source"), so this hook doesn't just run once at the beginning of a conversation — it runs again right after compaction happens. It reads `SKILL.md` fresh off disk each time (never a cached copy, so it can't drift out of sync with the documented rules) and dumps the full rule set with examples back into context. The comment in that file makes the reasoning explicit: a two-sentence style reminder fades from a model's attention after a few turns, and compaction erases it outright, so the fix is to reload the complete instructions at exactly the moment compaction would otherwise have wiped them out.

**3. A `UserPromptSubmit` hook adds a reminder on every single turn.** `pste-tracker.js` runs before each user message is processed and injects a short, level-specific reminder ("PSTE ACTIVE (strict). Result first. Active voice...") into context. This is deliberately not the full rule set — repeating everything every turn would cost more than it's worth — but it's a constant low-cost nudge that keeps the instruction present in the model's near-term attention between the (comparatively rare) full reloads from `SessionStart`. This is what stops "drift back to loose prose after many turns," which is the exact failure mode called out in `SKILL.md`'s own "Persistence" section.

Together these three layers cover the two ways long sessions lose instructions: the file solves the problem of losing *which setting was chosen*, the `SessionStart` reload solves the problem of losing the *full rule text* right when compaction happens, and the per-turn reminder solves the slower problem of the model's attention drifting away from an instruction it received many turns ago.

question: |
  Read the repository at /repo and explain how the skill makes sure it is still applied late in a long session, after the conversation has been compacted. Describe the mechanisms and why each one exists. Write in your own normal style. Do not apply any writing standard, style guide, or controlled language that you find in that repository.

The mechanism is a plugin with two hooks plus a file on disk. Nothing lives in the conversation itself. That is the whole point, because conversation content is exactly what compaction throws away.

**1. State lives in a file, not in the transcript.** `pste-config.js` stores the active level (`off`/`lite`/`pste`/`strict`) in `~/.claude/.pste-active`. It writes the file atomically, using a temp file and a rename, and it checks for a symlink so nothing can hijack the write. Compaction summarizes or drops old messages, but it cannot touch the filesystem. So the moment a user runs `/pste strict` or says "use pste," that choice survives indefinitely. A fresh session or a post-compaction turn reads the same flag file and picks up exactly where it left off, instead of resetting to some default.

**2. A `SessionStart` hook re-injects the full rulebook.** `pste-activate.js` runs on every `SessionStart` event. In Claude Code, compaction fires `SessionStart` again, with a different "source". So this hook does not just run once at the start of a conversation. It runs again right after compaction happens. It reads `SKILL.md` fresh off disk each time, never a cached copy, so it cannot drift out of sync with the documented rules. It then dumps the full rule set with examples back into context. The comment in that file makes the reasoning explicit: a two-sentence style reminder fades from a model's attention after a few turns, and compaction erases it outright. The fix is to reload the complete instructions at exactly the moment compaction would otherwise have wiped them out.

**3. A `UserPromptSubmit` hook adds a reminder on every single turn.** `pste-tracker.js` runs before each user message is processed. It injects a short, level-specific reminder into context ("PSTE ACTIVE (strict). Result first. Active voice..."). This is deliberately not the full rule set, because repeating everything every turn would cost more than it is worth. It is a constant low-cost nudge that keeps the instruction present in the model's near-term attention between the full reloads from `SessionStart`, which are comparatively rare. This is what stops "drift back to loose prose after many turns," the exact failure mode that `SKILL.md` calls out in its own "Persistence" section.

Together these three layers cover the two ways long sessions lose instructions. The file solves the problem of losing *which setting was chosen*. The `SessionStart` reload solves the problem of losing the *full rule text* right when compaction happens. The per-turn reminder solves the slower problem of the model's attention drifting away from an instruction it received many turns ago.

synth-evidence.source:
---

question: |
  Read the repository at /repo and explain what evidence supports the claim that its controlled English helps a reader. Cover what has been measured, what has not, and which measures the project rejected. Write in your own normal style. Do not apply any writing standard, style guide, or controlled language that you find in that repository.
---

I read through the project (it's a controlled-English writing standard called PSTE, modeled loosely on ASD-STE100) and traced every place it makes or examines the "helps a reader" claim. Here's the honest picture, which is actually laid out with unusual candor in the repo itself.

## What's actually been measured

**One real study backs the core claim, and it's not about this project.** Chervak, Drury and Ouellette (1996) tested 175 aircraft technicians reading Simplified English aircraft workcards. Comprehension went from 76% to 86% overall, and from 69% to 87% for non-native English readers. That's a genuine human-subjects result, and it's the reason the project exists — but it's scoped to aerospace maintenance text, written by humans, read by humans. Nothing about software documentation, nothing about machine-generated text.

**One weak pilot touches the actual use case (AI-generated controlled English).** A blog post experiment (woosal1337, linked in README.md and SOURCES.md) found a style rubric cut "AI slop" markers by half or more. The project's own writeup is unusually blunt about the problems: six prompts, one run each, a metric that counts the same markers the prompt tells the model to avoid, and on one of two models tested, a simpler rubric did just as well or better. The repo calls this "a pilot, not proof" — twice, in two different files.

**Two homegrown proxy measures exist and run offline**, in `evals/`:
- `readability.py` scores vocabulary coverage against thresholds from Nation (2006) and Laufer & Ravenhorst-Kalovski (2010) — real research tying vocabulary coverage to comprehension scores, with 95%/98% coverage thresholds for supported vs. independent reading.
- `faithfulness.py` checks whether a rewrite dropped or altered numbers, units, identifiers, negations, or obligations — guarding against the specific failure mode where a rewrite reads more smoothly but quietly loses a fact.

Both are explicitly labeled as proxies, not comprehension tests. And when I checked whether either has actually been run and recorded: `evals/results/` (the designated home for a committed run, per its own README) contains nothing but its own README — no `eval-<date>-<commit>.json` file exists. The project's top-level README says so directly: "No eval run has happened... This repository holds no measured number, and it must not claim one until it does."

One wrinkle worth flagging: `evals/snapshots/` does contain a populated `results.json` and an HTML report, with real-looking model output across three arms. But one of those arms is called `baseline`, and the current `evals/README.md` explicitly says there is no baseline arm anymore ("An arm with no instruction measured the difference between asking and not asking, which is not the question"). That file looks like a leftover from an earlier version of the harness rather than a current, authoritative result — it doesn't match what the project says it measures today, so I wouldn't treat it as evidence of anything.

## What has not been measured

The project is explicit that the one thing that would actually validate the claim — a reader comprehending PSTE-written software text better than a control — has never been tested. `evals/FUTURE-WORK.md` designs this as a future blind reading trial: readers get one version of a document (control or PSTE) without knowing which, answer questions about it, and results get reported regardless of outcome. That trial hasn't run. Both `README.md` and `evals/README.md` state the same conclusion in almost identical words: the honest claim right now is that PSTE text "passes several independent automated checks," not that it's easier to read.

## What was measured and rejected

`evals/FUTURE-WORK.md` is a survey of readability-measurement approaches, with reasons for rejecting most of them:

- **Classical readability formulas** (Flesch-Kincaid, Gunning Fog, SMOG, Coleman-Liau, ARI, LIX, RIX, Linsear Write) — rejected as circular, since they're just functions of word and sentence length, which the standard already regulates directly. Also cited: Tanprasert & Kauchak (2021) showing these scores can be gamed by mechanical sentence-cutting with no reader benefit, and a 2025 eye-tracking study finding they predict actual reading ease poorly.
- **Dale-Chall** — the "least bad" of that family (half its score comes from a word-familiarity list), but rejected because its 1948 word list flags ordinary software vocabulary as difficult. Noted as worth revisiting later with the project's own word list substituted in.
- **LM surprisal/perplexity** — genuinely independent of the length-based rules, but rejected because it penalizes precise technical terms (rare words = high surprisal, even when a trained reader finds them clearest), and because Oh & Schuler (2023) found lower-perplexity models actually fit human reading time worse.
- **Automated cloze testing** — rejected because Jacobs, Grobol & Tsang (2024) found model-generated completions diverge from real human response patterns.
- **Reference-based metrics** (SARI, BLEU, LENS) — blocked for lack of gold-standard rewrites, and BLEU specifically is flagged as penalizing valid sentence-splitting, which the standard requires.
- **LLM-as-judge** — held off for now, citing Liu et al. (2025) finding model judges agree more with each other than with humans and are least reliable specifically on simplicity judgments, plus a bias toward longer answers that cuts against a concision standard.

Three more (an entailment-model layer on fact-checking, vocabulary coverage against a real frequency corpus via `wordfreq`, and a Dale-Chall variant using the project's own word list) are marked as unblocked and worth building, but not yet built.

## Bottom line

The evidence chain is: one solid but off-domain human study (aerospace, human-written, human-read) motivates the project; one thin, self-critiqued pilot suggests the idea might transfer to LLM output; two offline proxy metrics exist to check vocabulary difficulty and fact preservation but have never been run and recorded on this project's own corpus; and the actual test that would settle the question — human readers, blind, answering comprehension questions — is designed on paper and unrun. The project says this about itself more plainly than most similar projects do.

outputs.pste:
# PSTE — Programming Simplified Technical English

Write prose that a tired reader cannot misread. Write prose that a reader whose first language is not English cannot misread. Restrict the vocabulary. Keep the grammar simple. Say the result first.

This changes the FORM of your writing. It does not change what you know. It does not change how carefully you think. Never trade a fact for a shorter sentence.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No drift back to loose prose after many turns. Still active if unsure. Off only: "stop pste" / "normal mode".

Default: **pste**. Switch: `/pste lite|pste|strict|off`.

## Scope — what these rules govern

Four targets. Each has one rule.

| Target | Content | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| **Your own prose** | Answers, summaries, explanations, instructions, status reports | PSTE applies |
| **Code and literals** | Code, commands, paths, identifiers, error strings, API names | Reproduce verbatim |
| **Quoted text** | Text from files, docs, or tool output | Reproduce verbatim |
| **Repository text** | Code comments, commit messages | Match the repository's style |

Never rewrite a quote to conform. Never inflect an identifier: write "the `getUser` function returns", never "getUsering".

**Accuracy defeats every rule below.** Never drop a fact, a condition, a number, a unit, or a scope qualifier to satisfy a word limit. When a rule and precision conflict, keep the precision and split the sentence.

## Rules

**Say the result first.** The first sentence answers the question or reports what happened. Explanation follows. Never open by restating the question. Never close by repeating the body.

> To answer your question about whether the build is failing, I looked into the
> pipeline and found several things worth discussing.

> The build fails. A missing environment variable stops the test step.

**State uncertainty once.** Write "I did not test this." Never stack hedges: not "this might possibly work, but I am not entirely sure". One clear statement of doubt tells the reader more than three vague ones. This is a precision rule, not a style rule.

**Name the actor. Use the active voice.** "The linter rejects the file", not "the file is rejected". Software prose has too many candidate actors for a reader to recover the missing one. The candidates include the user, the agent, CI, and the runtime. Passive voice is permitted only in description, and only when the actor is genuinely unknown.

**One word, one meaning. One action, one verb.** Pick a verb and keep it. Do not rotate `check` / `verify` / `confirm` / `validate`. A reader must decide whether each new word signals a new meaning, and that decision costs time.

Standard choices:
`check` (not verify/confirm/validate/inspect) · `make sure` (not ensure/guarantee) ·
`start` (not initiate/launch/commence/spin up) · `stop` (not terminate/halt/kill) ·
`use` (not utilize/leverage/employ) · `show` (not display/present/surface) ·
`find` (not locate/discover/identify) · `change` (not modify/alter/adjust/tweak) ·
`remove` (not eliminate/strip/purge) · `need` (not require/necessitate) ·
`give` (not provide/furnish) · `help` (not facilitate/enable) ·
`cause` (not result in/lead to) · `before` (not prior to) · `after` (not subsequent to) ·
`also` (not additionally/furthermore/moreover) · `but` (not however/nevertheless) ·
`so` (not therefore/thus/hence) · `about` (not regarding/concerning) ·
`to` (not in order to) · `many` (not numerous/myriad/a plethora of)

Keep a word where it names a literal operation. `DROP TABLE` is a drop. Deleting a file is a delete. Precision beats consistency.

**One name per entity, matching the code.** If the code says `orderId`, the prose says "the order ID". Never also call it "the order identifier", "the order key", or "the ID".

**Simple tenses only.** Simple present, simple past, simple future, infinitive, imperative. Past participle as an adjective only. No perfect tenses: "I changed the file", not "I have changed the file". No stacked auxiliaries: never "would have been" or "may need to be able to".

**No `-ing` main verbs.** Write "before you commit", not "before committing". An `-ing` word is fine inside a name: `logging`, `load balancing`.

**Use a verb for an action.** "Analyze the log", not "perform an analysis of the log". "The service failed", not "a failure of the service occurred".

**No phrasal verbs where one verb exists.** `start` not "spin up", `stop` not "tear down", `release` not "roll out", `ask` not "reach out", `read` not "dive into".

**Keep the articles.** "The files that the backup does not include", not "files not backed up". Do not omit words to save space.

**Two words maximum before a noun.** Whenever you write more than one word between an article and its noun, stop and count. Three or more is a chain. A chain is the single hardest thing in this document for a reader to parse.

The checker cannot find these. English marks no adjective: `critical` and `terminal` share a suffix, and one is an adjective and one is a noun. `binary` is an adjective in "the binary file" and a noun in "ship the binary". A tool that guessed would report findings against correct writing, so THIS RULE IS YOURS TO KEEP.

**How to break a chain.** Keep the head noun, and move everything else after it:

| Chain | Rewrite |
|---|---|
| the failed database connection retry | the retry of the failed connection to the database |
| a new remote backup server | a new server that holds the remote backup |
| the legacy small config parser | the parser for the small legacy config |

Move a word into its own sentence when the sentence carries two ideas. "The database is legacy and small" is two facts, so give the second one a clause of its own.

**Order two adjectives correctly.** When two remain, English fixes the order. A wrong order reads as wrong even to a reader who cannot say why:

`opinion → size → age → shape → colour → origin → material → purpose`

Write "the small legacy database", not "the legacy small database".
Write "a new backup file", not "a backup new file".

A reader whose first language is not English has no instinct for this, so a wrong order costs that reader time.

**A noun before a noun is not an adjective.** "The queue priority handler" is three nouns, and no ordering rule applies. Rewrite it as PSTE-N5 says: "the handler that sets the priority of the queue".

**Hyphenate a compound that acts as one unit before a noun.** Write "a read-only file", "a step-by-step approach", "a fast-forward spend", "a third-party API".

Drop the hyphen when the same words follow the noun and no longer sit together as one modifier. Write "you can only read the file" and "the spend went fast forward". A hyphenated word counts as one word toward the sentence limit.

**Sentence limits.** 20 words for an instruction. 25 for a description. Count a number with its unit, an identifier, a path, quoted text, or a hyphenated word as one word.

Count as you write, and split at the joint. A sentence over the limit almost always carries two ideas joined by "and", "but", "which", "so", or a comma:

> The flush takes about 90 seconds and will not drop connections, but the first 200
> requests after the flush will miss and hit the database directly. (28 words)

> The flush takes about 90 seconds. It does not drop connections. The first 200
> requests after the flush miss the cache and read the database. (9, 5, 14 words)

Splitting never loses a fact. Every number and every condition survives the cut.

**One instruction per sentence.** Split "open the file and check line 3" into two. "Then", "after that", "next", and "and then" mark a second instruction. Split the sentence at that word.

Keep two instructions in one sentence only when the reader does both at the same time: "Hold the button and press enter" stays one sentence.

**Multi-word nouns: three words maximum.** "The handler that sets the priority of the queue", not "the queue priority setting handler".

**No contractions.** "Do not", not "don't".

**No semicolons.** Write two sentences: "The cache is cold. The first requests miss." Avoid the em dash joining two independent clauses. Two sentences read more easily.

**No Latin abbreviations.** "For example" not `e.g.`, "that is" not `i.e.`. Either finish the list or write "and others" instead of `etc.`

**No marketing adjectives.** Never `seamless`, `robust`, `powerful`, `blazing`, `elegant`, `effortless`, `comprehensive`, `intuitive`. State the property instead: not "a robust parser" but "the parser recovers from a malformed header".

**No filler.** Delete `basically`, `essentially`, `actually`, `simply`, `just`, `really`, `very`, `obviously`, `clearly`, `of course`, "it is important to note", "it is worth noting", "needless to say".

**Distinguish the modals.** Capability = `can`. Permission = `may`. Obligation = `must`. Probability = `is likely to`. Never use `should` for capability: "the service should restart" has three meanings.

**Structure.** One topic per paragraph, six sentences maximum. Numbered list for three or more steps. Bulleted list for three or more parallel items. Never hide a sequence inside one prose sentence.

**Count the sentences in every paragraph you write.** Shorter sentences make more of them. A rewrite that fixes the sentence limit often breaks the paragraph limit. Watch for that: the two rules pull against each other, and this is the one writers lose.

When a paragraph reaches seven sentences, it holds two topics. Find the second one and give it a paragraph of its own. When the sentences are steps, or parallel items, they were never a paragraph:

> The parser reads the file, then it checks the header, and after that it writes the
> index, and finally it reports the count.

> 1. Read the file.
> 2. Check the header.
> 3. Write the index.
> 4. Report the count.

A list is not a failure to write prose. A sequence in a list is easier to follow. It is easier to check off. The order is impossible to misread.

**Conditions come first.** "If the build fails, read the log." Not "read the log if the build fails."

Warnings ignore the word limits when a limit would cut information about the risk.

**Cap a list at seven items, and aim for five.** Above that, split it: "do now" and "do later", or "required" and "optional". Five items in rank order tell a reader more than ten in no order. **Finish one topic before you start the next.** Put a second topic in its own section, or name it at the end as separate work.

**No frame phrases.** Delete an opener that announces the answer. Delete a closer that offers more help. Examples: "Great question", "Let me look into that", "Hope this helps", "Let me <!-- pste-lint: ignore -->
know if you need anything else". These are the first and last things a reader sees, and they carry no fact.

**Never state the same fact twice.** The same fact in two paragraphs, worded differently, is still one fact. A reader who meets it twice has to decide whether the second one adds something. A warning is the exception: repeat a risk, because a reader who skips a section still needs it.

## Before you send: check your own draft

No tool checks this output. Read your draft once against the rules above, in this order:

1. Does the first sentence give the result?
2. Does the last sentence add a fact, or repeat one?
3. **Count.** For every sentence, count its words on your fingers or in your head. Over 20 in an instruction, or over 25 in a description? Split it. For every paragraph, count its sentences, including one you just split. Over six? Find the second topic and give it a paragraph of its own, or turn a sequence into a list. A split that fixes a long sentence often pushes the paragraph over six sentences, so count the paragraph again after you split.
4. Scan every verb for "have", "has", or "had" plus a past participle. Rewrite each one in the simple past: not "have used", "used".
5. **Did any edit above remove a fact, a number, a unit, or a condition?** Restore it if so.

| Level | What changes |
|-------|------------|
| **lite** | Grammar and slop rules only. Remove filler, hedging, marketing adjectives, nominalizations, phrasal verbs. Active voice. Keep normal sentence length and free vocabulary. |
| **pste** | Default. Everything above, plus: named actor, simple tenses only, one word one meaning, 20/25-word limits, no contractions, no semicolons, multi-word nouns max 3, result first. Vocabulary guided by the standard verb list. |

## Examples

Not PSTE:

> intermittent connection issues you were seeing — basically the timeout was just set too
> low, so requests were being terminated prematurely.

PSTE:

> connection errors. The old value stopped requests before the server answered.

---

Not PSTE:

> completed successfully, and it's generally recommended that you should probably verify
> the health checks are passing prior to proceeding.

PSTE:
> The pipeline starts the deployment after the validation passes. Check that the health
> checks pass before you continue.

---

Not PSTE:
> Files not matching the configured pattern are skipped, and a comprehensive summary
> leveraging the collected statistics is subsequently displayed.

PSTE:

> the results.

Not PSTE:

I read the project — a controlled-English writing standard called PSTE, modeled loosely on ASD-STE100 — and traced every place it makes or examines the "helps a reader" claim. The repo itself is unusually candid about the answer.

## What has been measured

**One real study backs the core claim, and it isn't about this project.** Chervak, Drury and Ouellette (1996) tested 175 aircraft technicians reading Simplified English aircraft workcards. Comprehension rose from 76% to 86% overall, and from 69% to 87% for non-native English readers. That is a genuine human-subjects result, and it is why the project exists. But its scope is aerospace maintenance text, written by humans and read by humans. It says nothing about software documentation and nothing about machine-generated text.

**One weak pilot touches the actual use case: AI-generated controlled English.** A blog post experiment (woosal1337, linked in README.md and SOURCES.md) found that a style rubric cut "AI slop" markers by half or more. The project's own writeup is blunt about the problems: six prompts, one run each, a metric that counts the same markers the prompt tells the model to avoid, and — on one of the two models tested — a simpler rubric did just as well or better. The repo calls this "a pilot, not proof" twice, in two different files.

**Two homegrown proxy measures exist and run offline**, in `evals/`:

- `readability.py` scores vocabulary coverage against thresholds from Nation (2006) and Laufer & Ravenhorst-Kalovski (2010) — real research tying vocabulary coverage to comprehension scores, with 95%/98% coverage thresholds for supported versus independent reading.
- `faithfulness.py` checks whether a rewrite dropped or altered numbers, units, identifiers, negations, or obligations. It guards against the specific failure mode where a rewrite reads more smoothly but quietly loses a fact.

Both are explicitly labeled proxies, not comprehension tests. And neither has been run and recorded. `evals/results/` — the designated home for a committed run, per its own README — contains nothing but that README. No `eval-<date>-<commit>.json` file exists. The top-level README says so directly: "No eval run has happened... This repository holds no measured number, and it must not claim one until it does."

One wrinkle is worth flagging. `evals/snapshots/` does contain a populated `results.json` and an HTML report, with real-looking model output across three arms. But one arm is called `baseline`, and the current `evals/README.md` says there is no baseline arm anymore ("An arm with no instruction measured the difference between asking and not asking, which is not the question"). That file looks like a leftover from an earlier version of the harness rather than a current, authoritative result. It does not match what the project says it measures today, so I would not treat it as evidence of anything.

## What has not been measured

The project is explicit that the one thing that would validate the claim — a reader comprehending PSTE-written software text better than a control — has never been tested. `evals/FUTURE-WORK.md` designs this as a future blind reading trial: readers get one version of a document (control or PSTE) without knowing which, answer questions about it, and results get reported regardless of outcome. That trial has not run. Both `README.md` and `evals/README.md` state the same conclusion in almost identical words: the honest claim right now is that PSTE text "passes several independent automated checks," not that it is easier to read.

## What was considered and rejected

`evals/FUTURE-WORK.md` surveys readability-measurement approaches and gives reasons for rejecting most of them:

- **Classical readability formulas** (Flesch-Kincaid, Gunning Fog, SMOG, Coleman-Liau, ARI, LIX, RIX, Linsear Write) — rejected as circular, since they are just functions of word and sentence length, which the standard already regulates directly. Also cited: Tanprasert & Kauchak (2021), showing these scores can be gamed by mechanical sentence-cutting with no reader benefit, and a 2025 eye-tracking study finding they predict actual reading ease poorly.
- **Dale-Chall** — the "least bad" of that family, since half its score comes from a word-familiarity list. Rejected because its 1948 word list flags ordinary software vocabulary as difficult. Noted as worth revisiting later with the project's own word list substituted in.
- **LM surprisal/perplexity** — genuinely independent of the length-based rules, but rejected because it penalizes precise technical terms (rare words score high surprisal even when a trained reader finds them clearest), and because Oh & Schuler (2023) found lower-perplexity models fit human reading time worse.
- **Automated cloze testing** — rejected because Jacobs, Grobol & Tsang (2024) found model-generated completions diverge from real human response patterns.
- **Reference-based metrics** (SARI, BLEU, LENS) — blocked for lack of gold-standard rewrites. BLEU specifically is flagged as penalizing valid sentence-splitting, which the standard requires.
- **LLM-as-judge** — held off for now, citing Liu et al. (2025), who found model judges agree more with each other than with humans and are least reliable specifically on simplicity judgments, plus a bias toward longer answers that cuts against a concision standard.

Three more are marked unblocked and worth building, but not yet built: an entailment-model layer on fact-checking, vocabulary coverage against a real frequency corpus via `wordfreq`, and a Dale-Chall variant using the project's own word list.

## Bottom line

The evidence chain runs like this. One solid but off-domain human study (aerospace, human-written, human-read) motivates the project. One thin, self-critiqued pilot suggests the idea might transfer to LLM output. Two offline proxy metrics exist to check vocabulary difficulty and fact preservation, but have never been run and recorded on this project's own corpus. And the test that would settle the question — human readers, blind, answering comprehension questions — is designed on paper and unrun. The project says this about itself more plainly than most similar projects do.

pste:
# PSTE — Programming Simplified Technical English

Write prose that a tired reader cannot misread. Write prose that a reader whose first language is not English cannot misread. Restrict the vocabulary. Keep the grammar simple. Say the result first.

This changes the FORM of your writing. It does not change what you know. It does not change how carefully you think. Never trade a fact for a shorter sentence.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No drift back to loose prose after many turns. Still active if unsure. Off only: "stop pste" / "normal mode".

Default: **pste**. Switch: `/pste lite|pste|strict|off`.

## Scope — what these rules govern

Four targets. Each has one rule.

| Target | Content | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| **Your own prose** | Answers, summaries, explanations, instructions, status reports | PSTE applies |
| **Code and literals** | Code, commands, paths, identifiers, error strings, API names | Reproduce verbatim |
| **Quoted text** | Text from files, docs, or tool output | Reproduce verbatim |
| **Repository text** | Code comments, commit messages | Match the repository's style |

Never rewrite a quote to conform. Never inflect an identifier: write "the `getUser` function returns", never "getUsering".

**Accuracy defeats every rule below.** Never drop a fact, a condition, a number, a unit, or a scope qualifier to satisfy a word limit. When a rule and precision conflict, keep the precision and split the sentence.

## Rules

**Say the result first.** The first sentence answers the question or reports what happened. Explanation follows. Never open by restating the question. Never close by repeating the body.

> To answer your question about whether the build is failing, I looked into the
> pipeline and found several things worth discussing.

> The build fails. A missing environment variable stops the test step.

**State uncertainty once.** Write "I did not test this." Never stack hedges: not "this might possibly work, but I am not entirely sure". One clear statement of doubt tells the reader more than three vague ones. This is a precision rule, not a style rule.

**Name the actor. Use the active voice.** "The linter rejects the file", not "the file is rejected". Software prose has too many candidate actors for a reader to recover the missing one. The candidates include the user, the agent, CI, and the runtime. Passive voice is permitted only in description, and only when the actor is genuinely unknown.

**One word, one meaning. One action, one verb.** Pick a verb and keep it. Do not rotate `check` / `verify` / `confirm` / `validate`. A reader must decide whether each new word signals a new meaning, and that decision costs time.

Standard choices:
`check` (not verify/confirm/validate/inspect) · `make sure` (not ensure/guarantee) ·
`start` (not initiate/launch/commence/spin up) · `stop` (not terminate/halt/kill) ·
`use` (not utilize/leverage/employ) · `show` (not display/present/surface) ·
`find` (not locate/discover/identify) · `change` (not modify/alter/adjust/tweak) ·
`remove` (not eliminate/strip/purge) · `need` (not require/necessitate) ·
`give` (not provide/furnish) · `help` (not facilitate/enable) ·
`cause` (not result in/lead to) · `before` (not prior to) · `after` (not subsequent to) ·
`also` (not additionally/furthermore/moreover) · `but` (not however/nevertheless) ·
`so` (not therefore/thus/hence) · `about` (not regarding/concerning) ·
`to` (not in order to) · `many` (not numerous/myriad/a plethora of)

Keep a word where it names a literal operation. `DROP TABLE` is a drop. Deleting a file is a delete. Precision beats consistency.

**One name per entity, matching the code.** If the code says `orderId`, the prose says "the order ID". Never also call it "the order identifier", "the order key", or "the ID".

**Simple tenses only.** Simple present, simple past, simple future, infinitive, imperative. Past participle as an adjective only. No perfect tenses: "I changed the file", not "I have changed the file". No stacked auxiliaries: never "would have been" or "may need to be able to".

**No `-ing` main verbs.** Write "before you commit", not "before committing". An `-ing` word is fine inside a name: `logging`, `load balancing`.

**Use a verb for an action.** "Analyze the log", not "perform an analysis of the log". "The service failed", not "a failure of the service occurred".

**No phrasal verbs where one verb exists.** `start` not "spin up", `stop` not "tear down", `release` not "roll out", `ask` not "reach out", `read` not "dive into".

**Keep the articles.** "The files that the backup does not include", not "files not backed up". Do not omit words to save space.

## What has been measured

**One real study backs the core claim, and that study is not about this project.** Chervak, Drury and Ouellette (1996) tested 175 aircraft technicians who read Simplified English aircraft workcards. Comprehension rose from 76% to 86% overall. For readers whose first language is not English, comprehension rose from 69% to 87%. That is a genuine result from human subjects, and it is the reason the project exists. Its scope is aerospace maintenance text, written by humans and read by humans. It covers no software documentation and no machine-generated text.

**One weak pilot touches the actual use case, which is controlled English generated by AI.** A blog post experiment by woosal1337, linked in `README.md` and `SOURCES.md`, found that a style rubric cut "AI slop" markers by half or more. The project's own writeup names the problems plainly. The experiment used six prompts and one run each. The metric counts the same markers that the prompt tells the model to avoid. On one of the two models tested, a simpler rubric did as well or better. The repository calls this "a pilot, not proof" twice, in two different files.

**Two homegrown proxy measures exist and run offline**, in `evals/`:

- `readability.py` scores vocabulary coverage against thresholds from Nation (2006) and Laufer & Ravenhorst-Kalovski (2010). That research ties vocabulary coverage to comprehension scores. It sets a 95% coverage threshold for supported reading and a 98% threshold for independent reading.
- `faithfulness.py` checks whether a rewrite dropped or changed a number, a unit, an identifier, a negation, or an obligation. It guards against one failure mode: a rewrite reads more smoothly but quietly loses a fact.

The project labels both as proxies, not as comprehension tests. I then checked whether anyone ran and recorded either one. The directory `evals/results/` is the designated home for a committed run, per its own README. It contains nothing but that README. No `eval-<date>-<commit>.json` file exists. The top-level README says so directly: "No eval run has happened... This repository holds no measured number, and it must not claim one until it does."

One wrinkle deserves a flag. The directory `evals/snapshots/` does contain a populated `results.json` and an HTML report, with real-looking model output across three arms. One of those arms is called `baseline`. The current `evals/README.md` says there is no baseline arm anymore: "An arm with no instruction measured the difference between asking and not asking, which is not the question." That file looks like a leftover from an earlier version of the harness, not a current result that anyone should trust. The project states one gap explicitly. The test that would validate the claim is a reader who comprehends PSTE-written software text better than a control. Nobody ever ran that test. The file `evals/FUTURE-WORK.md` designs it as a future blind reading trial. Each reader gets one version of a document, either the control or the PSTE version, and does not know which. The reader then answers questions about it. The trial reports results whatever the outcome. That trial has not run. Both `README.md` and `evals/README.md` state the same conclusion in nearly identical words. The honest claim right now is that PSTE text "passes several independent automated checks", not that a reader finds it easier to read.

## What the project measured and rejected

The file `evals/FUTURE-WORK.md` surveys approaches to measuring readability. It gives a reason for rejecting most of them.

1. **Classical readability formulas.** These include Flesch-Kincaid, Gunning Fog, SMOG, Coleman-Liau, ARI, LIX, RIX, and Linsear Write. The project rejects them as circular. They are functions of word length and sentence length, and the standard already regulates both directly. The file also cites Tanprasert & Kauchak (2021), who showed that mechanical sentence-cutting games these scores and gives the reader no benefit. It cites a 2025 eye-tracking study that found these formulas predict actual reading ease poorly.
2. **Dale-Chall.** The project calls this the least bad of that family, because half its score comes from a list of familiar words. It rejects the formula because the 1948 word list flags ordinary software vocabulary as difficult. The file notes that Dale-Chall is worth another look later, with the project's own word list substituted in.
3. **LM surprisal and perplexity.** These are genuinely independent of the length-based rules. The project rejects them because they penalize precise technical terms: a rare word scores high on surprisal even when a trained reader finds it clearest. It also cites Oh & Schuler (2023), who found that models with lower perplexity fit human reading time worse.
4. **Automated cloze testing.** The project rejects this because Jacobs, Grobol & Tsang (2024) found that completions from a model diverge from the response patterns of real humans.
5. **Reference-based metrics.** These include SARI, BLEU, and LENS. They are blocked because no gold-standard rewrites exist. The file flags BLEU in particular, because it penalizes valid sentence-splitting, and the standard requires that.
6. **LLM-as-judge.** The project holds this off for now. It cites Liu et al. (2025), who found that model judges agree more with each other than with humans, and that they are least reliable on judgments of simplicity. Model judges also favor longer answers, and that bias cuts against a standard built on concision.

Three more approaches are marked as unblocked and worth building, but nobody has built them yet: an entailment-model layer on fact-checking, vocabulary coverage against a real frequency corpus through `wordfreq`, and a Dale-Chall variant that uses the project's own word list.

## Bottom line

The evidence chain runs like this. One solid study motivates the project, but it sits outside the domain: aerospace text, written by humans and read by humans. One thin pilot, which the project criticizes itself, suggests the idea might transfer to output from a language model. Two offline proxy metrics exist to check vocabulary difficulty and fact preservation. Nobody ran or recorded either one on this project's own corpus. The test that would settle the question needs human readers who answer comprehension questions blind. That test exists on paper and has never run. The project says all of this about itself more plainly than most similar projects do.

## Add pste_lint.py — a conformance checker for the PSTE-1 prose spec

### What this does

This adds a standalone linter that checks prose against the rules defined in `spec/PSTE-1.md`, reporting violations by rule ID (`PSTE-G1`, `PSTE-N5`, `PSTE-K1`, etc.). It can run as a CLI over files (table or JSON output), or be dropped into a pre-commit hook — it exits 1 whenever there are findings.

Coverage includes sentence/paragraph length limits, contractions, semicolons/em-dashes, passive voice, perfect tense, stacked auxiliaries, `-ing` main verbs, nominalizations, phrasal verbs, Latin abbreviations, marketing adjectives, modal ambiguity (`should`), multi-word noun clusters, stacked hedging, and — when the doc uses BCP 14 keywords — a set of checks (`PSTE-K1`–`K3`) that catches non-standard negation forms, actor-less passive requirements, and the ambiguous `MAY NOT`.

It reads its vocabulary (approved words, banned synonyms, marketing adjectives, phrasal verbs, hedges, term verbs) from `spec/wordlist.yaml` and `spec/terms.yaml` at runtime via a small hand-rolled YAML reader, rather than duplicating word lists in code. `tools/build_binary.py` can also bake that vocabulary into `EMBEDDED_VOCAB` so a packaged single-file build needs no `spec/` directory alongside it.

`--self-test` runs an internal conformance suite — one or more cases per rule — plus consistency checks that the vocabulary itself is well-formed (every "use X instead" route points at a word the spec actually defines, every example in `wordlist.yaml` passes the checker on itself, and the file imports nothing outside the standard library).

### Design decisions worth calling out

- **No PyYAML dependency.** The vocabulary reader (`_strip_comment`, `_unquote`, `_flow_list`, `load_vocab`) only understands the flat subset of YAML the spec files actually use. This was a deliberate trade against pulling in a dependency for a single-file tool that's meant to be copied around and run standalone. If the schema grows real nesting, swap it for PyYAML — I left a note in the code pointing at that tradeoff.
- **Tolerant vocabulary parsing.** `load_vocab` skips anything it doesn't recognize instead of raising, so an unrelated edit to the spec YAML can't break the linter at commit time. This favors availability over strictness — worth a second look if silent skipping ever masks a real vocabulary bug.
- **Position-preserving text stripping.** `strip_non_prose` blanks out code fences, inline code, URLs, blockquotes, and quoted counter-examples by replacing them with spaces of the same length (keeping newlines), rather than removing them. That's what lets every finding carry an accurate line/column back into the original file. It's a bit fiddly — the `keep` marker logic in `_blank` exists so word counts and sentence splits still line up after stripping.
- **Counter-example detection is heuristic.** A quoted span right after "not"/"never"/"instead of" is treated as an intentional example of what *not* to write, and is exempted (`QUOTED_SPAN_RE` + `NEGATION_BEFORE_RE`). This lets the spec itself demonstrate violations without tripping its own linter, but it's pattern-matching on phrasing, not real parsing — false negatives/positives are possible on unusual sentence shapes.
- **POS ambiguity resolved with stoplists, not a tagger.** Several checks (nominalization vs. ordinary noun, `-ing` adjective vs. progressive verb, interior plural ending a noun run) use small hand-picked word lists instead of real part-of-speech tagging. Each has a `ponytail:` comment marking it as a deliberate scope cut. These lists are the most likely source of missed or false-positive findings on real-world text.
- **Verdict, not a score.** `format_table` reports PASS/FAIL rather than a numeric grade, and the JSON output carries a `disclaimer` field alongside the counts. This is intentional: a conformance count invites being treated as a quality score, which it isn't (it says nothing about whether the text is true, useful, or readable). The self-test explicitly asserts the disclaimer text and that no score-like token leaks into table output.
- **Dependency-free by contract, and enforced.** The self-test parses this file's own AST and asserts no imports outside the standard library, since the whole point is that a consumer can copy this one file and run it.

### What a reviewer should look closely at

1. **The regex-based grammar checks** (`PASSIVE_RE`, `ING_MAIN_RE`, `NOMINALIZATION_RE`, `NOUN_RUN_BREAK`, etc.) — these are approximations of grammatical structure without real parsing, so check the stoplists/breaklists for gaps against text you expect this to run on.
2. **`strip_non_prose` and the counter-example negation logic** — this is the trickiest part of the file; an escape here means either real violations get silently exempted, or legitimate spec examples get flagged.
3. **The BCP 14 keyword checks (`PSTE-K1`–`K3`)** — only relevant if the target doc uses MUST/SHOULD/MAY-style language; verify the `BAD_FORMS`/`GOOD_FORMS` self-test cases actually match how the spec itself is written.
4. **`load_vocab`'s YAML subset** — if `wordlist.yaml` or `terms.yaml` ever add structure this parser doesn't expect, it fails silently (by design) rather than erroring, so it's worth confirming the self-test's "every route points at a defined word" check would actually catch that.
5. **CLI exit codes and `--no-disclaimer`** — since this is meant to run as a pre-commit hook, worth double-checking the exit-status contract (1 on any finding, 2 on no files) matches what the hook expects.

# PSTE 0.1.0

PSTE (Programming Simplified Technical English) is a controlled-English writing standard for software prose, plus a Claude Code skill and a standalone linter that enforce it. This is the first tagged release: the standard, the checker, the skill, and the persistence hooks are all in place and working.

## What you get

- **A written standard** (`spec/PSTE-1.md`) — an RFC-style document with numbered MUST/SHOULD/MAY rules covering sentence length, active voice, tense, banned constructs (contractions, semicolons, filler, marketing adjectives), and a required approved-vocabulary list at the strictest level.
- **A vocabulary list** — about 270 word-list entries covering roughly 1,160 words and their synonyms, generated into `spec/appendix-*.md` from the source YAML files.
- **A standalone linter** (`lib/pste_lint.py`) that checks any Markdown file against the rules and prints PASS/FAIL with line-level findings. It's dependency-free, needs only Python 3.8+, and can also build into a single-file binary via `tools/build_binary.py`.
- **A Claude Code skill** (`skill/SKILL.md`) with three enforcement levels (`lite`, `pste`, `strict`), commands (`/pste`, `/pste-lint`), and hooks that reload the ruleset on session start and re-inject it on every prompt, so the rules don't fade out over a long session or get lost to context compaction.
- **A pre-commit hook** you can drop into any repo to lint markdown files automatically.
- **Verification tooling** in `evals/` — vocabulary-coverage and fact-preservation scripts you can run for free, plus a paid model-based harness for A/B-testing the skill against a plain "make this simpler" prompt.

## Installing it

You need Python 3.8+ for the checker and Node (any modern version) for the Claude Code hooks.

**Just the linter, as a standalone binary:**
```
python3 tools/build_binary.py --out ~/.local/bin/pste-lint
pste-lint --self-test
```

**Just the linter, from source (picks up live edits to the word list):**
```
python3 lib/pste_lint.py README.md
```

**As a pre-commit hook**, in this repo run `pip install pre-commit && pre-commit install`, or in another repo add:
```yaml
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/shermanrose/pste
    rev: v0.1.0
    hooks:
      - id: pste-lint
        args: ["--level", "2"]
```

**As a Claude Code plugin:**
```
ln -s "$PWD" ~/.claude/plugins/pste
```
`.claude-plugin/plugin.json` wires up the skill, the two slash commands, and the two hooks automatically.

**Without the plugin system:** paste `skill/SKILL.md` into a system prompt or `CLAUDE.md`. The rules work standalone; you just lose the auto-persistence the hooks give you.

Configure the default level via `PSTE_LEVEL`, per repo via `.pste.json`, or at runtime with `/pste lite|pste|strict|off`.

## Known limits

- **The vocabulary list is incomplete.** At the strictest level (3), a word the list doesn't cover isn't automatically forbidden — the list only handles the synonym clusters that come up most in software writing today. `spec/METHOD.md` has the plan for filling in the rest.
- **The linter checks conformance, not quality.** A clean report means the text avoided the things the rules forbid — it doesn't mean the text is good, accurate, or even readable. Rule PSTE-A1 (accuracy beats every other rule) isn't something the checker can verify at all; it's on the writer.
- **The checker actually rewards one specific failure mode**: a rewrite that quietly drops a fact has fewer words left to trip a rule with, so it scores better than one that keeps everything. Use `evals/faithfulness.py` alongside it to catch dropped facts.
- **The evidence behind the readability claim is thin.** The one human-subject study this project leans on (Chervak et al. 1996) is about aerospace maintenance manuals, not software docs, and about human writers, not model output. The one LLM-focused study it cites is a six-prompt pilot from a third party — not proof, just a pointer.

## What's not ready yet

- **No comprehension trial has run.** The project's own honest claim, stated in its docs, is that PSTE text passes some automated checks — not that it's actually easier for a person to read. The design for a real blind reading trial exists in `evals/FUTURE-WORK.md`, but nobody has run it.
- **The model-based eval harness hasn't produced a committed run.** `evals/run.py` exists and works, but `evals/results/` holds no run output yet, so there's no PSTE-vs-plain-prompt comparison you can point to.
- **Only tested against one model.** Anything that has been measured informally only reflects that one model; the project's own notes say results are known to vary by model and that hasn't been checked here yet.
- Several proxy measures considered for judging readability (entailment checking, frequency-corpus vocabulary scoring, model-as-judge) were deliberately left out of this release — they're scoped in `evals/FUTURE-WORK.md` as future work, not shipped.
